name: Pink orchid
lede: Pink Orchid is a medium, slightly purple pink named for the flower, a shade closer to magenta than to the pale pink of a carnation.

sections.title: A flower's pink, not a dye's
sections.body:
Our library traces the name only to a Wikipedia color list, which gives no date for its coining and no citation to a dictionary of color [1]. Orchid flowers range from near-white to deep magenta, so "Pink Orchid" names one slice of that range rather than a single species [1]. In printed English the phrase peaked in the 2010s and has risen since 2000, a recent rise consistent with a cosmetics or fashion-marketing name rather than an old dye term [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[light-rosolane-purple]], 3.2 units of CIEDE2000 away and more vivid [1]. [[light-mallow-purple]] sits a little farther out at 4.9, also more vivid and lighter, and [[persian-pink]] at 5.1 [1]. Measured in LCH, it sits at lightness 65 with strong chroma, among the more saturated pinks in our library [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive has this exact color covering at least one percent of its canvas, as photographed [2]. That absence describes this particular archive of museum paintings, not painting as a whole, and is consistent with a recently popular name for a shade better known from flowers, cosmetics and fabric than from old oil paint [2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [2].

openers: Pink Orchid is closer to magenta than to a pale carnation pink, and its printed use has risen mostly since 2000.

issues: The cosmetics/fashion-marketing inference is a reasonable reading of the Ngram rise, not a documented sourced claim.
